prize_parts.citation: for empirical analysis of how trade and technological change reshape labour demand, local labour markets and wage inequality

statement.case_for: B019 addresses a first-order question: why adjustment to trade and technology shocks was slower and more concentrated than the standard model suggested. It does so with transparent, quasi-experimental designs that other researchers have re-analysed extensively, and the broad conclusion has held up. The China-shock papers by Autor, Dorn and Hanson are a coherent, jointly authored body of work. Autor's task-based framework supplies the conceptual interpretation. My own field makes me value work whose identifying assumptions are explicit and have survived independent scrutiny, but I treat that as one consideration among the common criteria. The influence on labour, trade and public economics, and on policy debate, is large. The core papers are now a decade or more old, so timing is not a concern. I keep the citation on empirical analysis of adjustment to trade and technological change, not on the whole task-based theory literature. That way it credits what the three named people most clearly did and does not claim more than the attribution supports.
statement.case_against: The magnitude and long-run persistence of the China-shock effects are still debated, and the shift-share exposure designs rest on identifying assumptions that are contested. The three-name cap also forces exclusions. Katz has a credible claim through the skill-demand work, and the task framework has co-originators outside this ballot entry. A citation that spans both the trade-shock and task strands could look like two contributions stitched together. If the committee weighs conceptual depth over empirical design, B001 is the more theory-centred option and has clean two-person attribution.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B019 third and proposes only Autor and Hanson. He cites debate over exposure measures, shift-share identification and long-run persistence. He also notes that Katz's skill-biased-change work overlaps with already recognised work and that the task framework has co-originators outside the credited set.
responses.response: The identification concerns are real, and I list them as unresolved. I read the fact that independent researchers have stress-tested these designs, and the broad finding of persistent local adjustment costs has survived, as support for the contribution, not a mark against it. I disagree on dropping Dorn. The China-shock papers are a joint Autor-Dorn-Hanson body of work, and leaving out Dorn would create an attribution gap in the part of the case where credit is clearest. I agree that Katz's overlap with prior recognition weakens the case for a Katz slot.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B019 fourth and proposes Autor, Katz and Hanson. He stresses the policy influence of the task and trade-shock work. He also notes that Acemoglu-Restrepo is a related task theory and that the grouping is a judgment about which contributions to credit.
responses.response: I accept that Katz is a legitimate alternative third name, and I mark that as uncertain. I still prefer Dorn because the citation I propose rests on the China-shock evidence on local labour-market adjustment, and Dorn is a co-author of that core work. Your Acemoglu-Restrepo point reinforces my narrower framing. A citation built on empirical analysis of adjustment to trade and technological change avoids claiming the whole task-theory literature. I agree that the credit boundary is a judgment call and not a settled fact.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B001 first. She argues the Grossman-Helpman partnership is a clean two-person attribution, with decades of confirmation and broad, durable influence on trade theory and political economy. She also ranks B019 second, as 'big question' work.
responses.response: I agree on attribution and maturity, which is why B001 is my second choice and a named alternative. Where I differ is in weighting the empirical record. Both of you note that support for the protection-for-sale predictions is mixed, and for me a framework's influence is stronger when its core claims have been tested directly. B019's central claims have been tested heavily and have largely held in broad outline. The extra overlap of Helpman with B020 also leaves open how the committee would frame a B001 award. I do not think B001 is weaker on merit. My ranking reflects a different weighting of the evidence base.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B019 seventh, behind B001, B016 and B031. He questions the magnitude and persistence of the China shock and the attribution split between the task framework and the trade-shock work.
responses.response: Both concerns are fair and I share them. They are why I keep Katz and the task-framework credit in the uncertainties and limit the citation to what the three named people most directly did. I would add that debate over magnitude is not the same as doubt about the finding. The qualitative result, that adjustment was slow and geographically concentrated, is robust to the main critiques as I understand them, though I have not independently verified this. I agree the committee should not treat the trade and task strands as one achievement without saying so.

uncertainties: Whether the long-run persistence and magnitude of the China-shock effects, and the validity of shift-share exposure designs, are settled well enough for a prize citation.
Whether Katz should replace Dorn, and how to credit the task framework, which has co-originators outside this ballot entry.
Whether the committee sees the task and trade-shock strands as one coherent achievement or as two distinct contributions.
How far B001 and B014 should be preferred if colleagues weigh conceptual depth or maturity differently from me.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The profile lists no co-authorship, institutional or editorial tie to any credited name on B019, B001 or B014.
